label: HTTP service
summary: The server's own view of the requests: rate, 5xx share, mean, slowest and p95 latency
source: Micrometer's http.server.requests timer as Spring Boot Actuator records it for Spring MVC and WebFlux, under Micrometer's Prometheus names (http_server_requests_seconds_count, _sum and _max, and _bucket with a histogram): Spring Framework's server request observation convention (tags error, exception, method, outcome, status, uri; status is the raw response code), Spring Boot 4.1.1's metrics reference and Micrometer's PrometheusNamingConvention, MicrometerCollector, AbstractTimerBuilder and DistributionStatisticConfig at main, read on 2026-10-09; the queries were not run against a live service. A service whose timer was renamed (management.observations.http.server.requests.name), one on Spring's OpenTelemetry convention (http.server.request.duration) and one on another framework need a custom query. Prometheus' own scrapes of the actuator count as requests. latency.p95 needs management.metrics.distribution.percentiles-histogram.http.server.requests=true, without which there is no _bucket series; a timer's histogram's top bucket is maximum-expected-value, 30 s unless the service sets it lower or higher, and a quantile reads no further than it: a quantile at that bound means at least that. At the other end, below minimum-expected-value (1 ms by default) a quantile is a fraction of the first bucket. Only the computed quantile reaches the report, never the buckets, so neither end can be marked. _max is the slowest request in Micrometer's decaying window, 2 minutes by default, so the run's first scrapes can carry a request from before it. Micrometer creates a timer for a tag set the first time it records one (DefaultMeterObservationHandler's onStop), and status is a tag, so a service that has returned no 5xx since it started has no 5xx series: errors.5xx.pct reads 0 for it rather than nothing (the 'or 0 *' fallback), and when a 5xx status first appears, its new series starts at the count its first scrape sees, which rate() takes as the baseline, so those first 5xx are not counted. In-flight requests are left out: Micrometer 1.18's DefaultMeterObservationHandler builder no longer creates the http.server.requests.active timer unless asked, and Spring Boot 3.3 added management.observations.long-task-timer.enabled to switch it off, so whether the series exists depends on the versions. No tool's name is given: Datadog's APM metrics embed the span name (trace.<SPAN_NAME>.hits, .errors, and the trace.<SPAN_NAME> distribution), which depends on the integration, so each is null; OpenTelemetry's http.server.request.duration (Stable, seconds) is a histogram, and the rate, the 5xx share, the mean and the p95 are each computed from it, so each is null; Telegraf reads a Micrometer endpoint only through inputs.prometheus, whose names depend on its metric_version. Export the computed series under the catalogue's name.

metrics.name: requests.rate
metrics.label: Requests per second (avg)
metrics.description: Requests the service finished per second, averaged over the run: it shows the load reached this service. Compare it with JMeter's own rate; a shortfall means something in front answered, refused or queued the rest.

metrics.name: errors.5xx.pct
metrics.label: Server errors, 5xx (%)
metrics.description: Requests answered with a 5xx status, as a percentage of all requests, in the worst minute. It separates the service's own failures from errors JMeter met in front of it, at a load balancer or a gateway. The first 5xx of a status the service had not returned since it started are not counted: they start its series.

queries.prometheus: 100 * (sum by (instance) (rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{status=~"5.."${andMatch}}[1m])) or 0 * sum by (instance) (rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count${match}[1m]))) / sum by (instance) (rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count${match}[1m]))

metrics.name: latency.mean
metrics.label: Mean response time (ms)
metrics.description: Mean time the service took per request, in the worst minute, measured inside the application. Set beside JMeter's own times, the difference is spent in the network, a proxy or a queue in front of it.

metrics.name: latency.max
metrics.label: Slowest request (ms)
metrics.description: The slowest request the service served during the run, or up to 2 minutes before it, measured inside the application. A single outlier sets it, so compare it with JMeter's own maximum rather than judging it alone.

metrics.name: latency.p95
metrics.label: Response time p95 (ms)
metrics.description: 95th percentile of the time the service took per request, in the worst minute. Needs the request histogram, which Spring Boot leaves off: set management.metrics.distribution.percentiles-histogram.http.server.requests=true, or this metric has no data.
